problemText: Marco Polo describes the palace of Kublai Khan, the Mongol founder of China's Yuan Dynasty, at Cambaluc: the hall could "dine 6000 people" and the building was "so vast, so rich, and so beautiful, that no man on earth could design anything superior to it." This description is best used as evidence that —
choices: The Mongol Yuan Dynasty preserved the civil-service examination system fully intact from Song times, unchanged after 1279
Song China's commercial economy collapsed entirely once the Mongols completed their conquest in 1279
Yuan rule continued the same scale of centralized Chinese imperial grandeur Song China had built, despite being a foreign dynasty
Kublai Khan built his palace using techniques and materials borrowed entirely from Mongol steppe architecture, with no continuity from Chinese imperial tradition
hints: Notice this is the Yuan court under Kublai Khan, a Mongol ruler — not a Song emperor — even though the scale of the palace echoes centuries of Chinese imperial tradition.

Rule out any answer describing economic collapse, an unchanged exam system, or a total break from earlier Chinese building traditions — the passage is about continuity of scale under new, foreign rule.

problemText: Marco Polo adds that the palace roof's colors were "fixed with a varnish so fine and exquisite that they shine like crystal, and lend a resplendent lustre to the Palace as seen for a great way round." Writing for a European audience with no comparable frame of reference, this vivid, admiring description is best explained by which point about Marco Polo as a historical source?
choices: He was a technically trained architect providing a precise structural assessment of Yuan-era construction methods
He wrote as an impressed foreign merchant conveying an outsider's admiration, not delivering a technical architectural verdict
He served as a Yuan court official whose official duties required him to praise the palace in writing
He was quoting an earlier Song Dynasty account of the same palace rather than describing what he personally observed
hints: Think about who Marco Polo was — a Venetian merchant, not an architect or a Yuan official — describing something new to him for readers back home.
Rule out any answer that turns Polo into a technical expert or an official mouthpiece — his language here is the color of personal amazement.

problemText: The Song Dynasty's civil-service examination system tested candidates on mastery of the Confucian classics and, in principle, was open to any male subject regardless of birth. Which statement best captures how this system actually functioned in practice?
choices: It was open equally to men and women of every social class, with the state fully subsidizing all exam preparation
It restricted government office exclusively to hereditary aristocratic families, with the exam serving only a ceremonial function
It was a meritocratic ideal that somewhat expanded mobility, but in practice favored wealthy families able to afford classical education
It was abolished entirely once the Mongols completed their conquest of China in 1279, and was never restored afterward
hints: Separate the exam system's formal, in-principle openness from how much it actually cost, in time and money, to prepare for it.
The Yuan did suspend the exams after 1279 — but they partially restored a version of them in 1315, so 'never restored' overstates the change.

problemText: In 1258, Mongol forces sacked Baghdad and executed the last Abbasid caliph who resided there, ending a roughly five-century-old political and religious center. Historians characterize this event as ending which of the following?
choices: All Muslim political authority anywhere in the Dar al-Islam, since no Muslim-ruled state successfully resisted the Mongols afterward
The ulama's shared madrasa curriculum and Sufi religious networks, which depended entirely on the Baghdad caliph's continued rule
The spread of Islam into South and Southeast Asia, which had relied exclusively on the Abbasid caliphate's direct political sponsorship
Baghdad's own run as a political and religious capital — not the Dar al-Islam's broader coherence, which had many other centers of power by then
hints: Political power in the Dar al-Islam had already fragmented into regional sultanates — Seljuk, Mamluk, Delhi — well before 1258; the Mamluks even defeated the Mongols in 1260.
Keep the fall of ONE institution in Baghdad analytically separate from the ulama, madrasa, and Sufi networks that connected Muslims across political boundaries.

problemText: Ibn Battuta describes his reception at the court of Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq of Delhi: after appointing him qadi (judge), the Sultan bestowed on him "a dress of honour, and a horse furnished with an ornamented saddle" along with a salary "drawn from the treasury." This account is best used as evidence that the Delhi Sultanate —
choices: relied on lavish court patronage — robes, mounts, salaried appointments — to recruit foreign-born scholars into its service
restricted every administrative office and government appointment exclusively to native-born Hindu subjects, excluding foreign Muslim travelers entirely
had no functioning royal treasury at all and compensated its officials only through ceremonial gifts rather than any real ongoing salary
required foreign travelers to renounce their homelands permanently before receiving any court appointment
hints: Notice what the Sultan actually gave Ibn Battuta: a robe, a horse, and a paid appointment — think about what that combination was meant to secure.
Rule out any answer claiming the sultanate excluded foreigners or had no real treasury — the passage shows the opposite.

problemText: Ibn Battuta describes Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq as "one of the most bountiful and splendidly munificent men" yet also "one of the most impetuous and inexorable: and very seldom indeed did it happen, that pardon followed his anger." This portrait of a single, dramatic ruler is best used as evidence for which point about the Delhi Sultanate?
choices: Islam had spread across the Indian subcontinent primarily through the Sultan's military campaigns rather than through merchants and Sufi teachers
The Sultan's generosity and anger were recorded identically by every foreign visitor to his court
The Delhi Sultanate's Hindu-majority population held equal political power alongside its Turkic Muslim rulers
Political authority in the sultanate rested heavily on the sultan's unpredictable personal favor rather than on fixed, impersonal legal procedure
hints: Think about what it means for a single ruler's mood to swing between extreme generosity and merciless anger, with 'seldom' any pardon.
This item is about the nature of the Sultan's personal power, not about how Islam spread or about Hindu-Muslim power-sharing.

problemText: In his 1520 letter to Charles V, the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés describes the Mexica capital, Tenochtitlan: "There is one square, twice as large as that of Salamanca, all surrounded by arcades, where there are daily more than sixty thousand souls, buying and selling" This description is best used as evidence that —
choices: the Mexica were an isolated, loosely organized society with no significant markets or large-scale trade before European contact
Cortés found Tenochtitlan's markets smaller and less developed than those of contemporary Spanish cities
Tenochtitlan supported large-scale, sustained commercial activity befitting the capital of a powerful, centrally organized tribute empire
Spanish soldiers had already destroyed Tenochtitlan's marketplace by the time Cortés wrote this letter
hints: Sixty thousand people buying and selling daily in one square alone is evidence of the scale of commerce a capital city like Tenochtitlan supported.
Rule out any answer describing the Mexica as isolated, primitive, or already destroyed — Cortés is describing a thriving city he personally observed.

problemText: The Catalan Atlas (1375), made by the Majorcan cartographer Abraham Cresques for the king of Aragon, captions its image of the Mali ruler Mansa Musa: "this king is the richest and most noble lord of all this region on account of the abundance of gold that is gathered in his land." Made decades after Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj, this caption most directly —
choices: confirms, independently of any African source, that Mali's wealth and power were already recognized abroad
proves that Cresques personally traveled to Mali's court to interview Mansa Musa about his kingdom's finances
shows that Aragon's king had negotiated a formal treaty guaranteeing annual gold shipments from Mali
demonstrates that Mali's rulers commissioned the map themselves to advertise their wealth to Europe
hints: The Atlas was made by a European cartographer for a European king, decades after the hajj — think about what that tells you about Mali's reputation outside Africa.
Rule out any answer requiring Cresques to have visited Mali himself or a formal Aragon-Mali treaty — the caption is evidence of reputation, not diplomacy.

problemText: Magna Carta (1215), clause 12, states: "No scutage not aid shall be imposed on our kingdom, unless by common counsel of our kingdom" This clause is best used as evidence that Magna Carta —
choices: eliminated the English monarchy entirely in favor of rule by an assembly of barons
limited the king's power to levy certain taxes without his barons' consent
granted ordinary peasants the right to vote on all new royal taxes
abolished the feudal practice of scutage altogether, for any reason
hints: 'Unless by common counsel of our kingdom' is a procedural limit on the king's power to tax, not an abolition of the monarchy.
Note the clause still permits scutage/aid in named cases (ransom, knighting the eldest son, marrying the eldest daughter) — it limits, rather than abolishes, the practice.

problemText: Magna Carta further provides: "No freemen shall be taken or imprisoned or disseised or exiled or in any way destroyed, nor will we go upon him nor send upon him, except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land." and "To no one will we sell, to no one will we refuse or delay, right or justice." These clauses are best interpreted as —
choices: a limit on arbitrary royal justice for free subjects, not a grant of democracy to the whole population
a full establishment of representative democracy in which all English subjects, including serfs, could vote
a permanent transfer of all judicial authority from the king to the Catholic Church
proof that thirteenth-century England had already abolished the feudal system entirely
hints: Notice the clause protects 'freemen' specifically — medieval England still had a large unfree (serf) population outside this protection.
Rule out any answer describing full democracy, church takeover of justice, or the end of feudalism — the clause limits royal power over free subjects, nothing more.

problemText: The Mexica Empire administered conquered altepetl (city-states) chiefly by requiring regular tribute in goods, labor, or captives while leaving local rulers largely in place. The Inca Empire, by contrast, administered its territory chiefly through the mit'a system of rotational labor service, reinforced by an extensive road network and quipu record-keeping. Which statement best distinguishes these two administrative models?
choices: The Inca required conquered city-states to pay tribute in goods and captives, while the Mexica organized subject labor through rotational mit'a service
The Mexica extracted tribute from largely self-governing subordinate city-states, while the Inca organized subject communities' labor time directly through the mit'a system
Both empires relied on the same rotational corvée-labor system, differing only in which specific crops each region's farmers were assigned to the state
The Mexica left conquered altepetl with no ongoing obligations to Tenochtitlan at all, while only the Inca imposed any formal administrative requirements on subject peoples
hints: Keep the two systems distinct: tribute extraction from largely autonomous polities versus direct organization of subject labor time.
Rule out any answer that swaps the two systems between empires, treats them as identical, or claims the Mexica imposed no obligations at all.

problemText: Cahokia, a large Mississippian urban center near the confluence of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, reached its peak population and regional influence roughly 1050-1200, and was already in decline during the 1200-1450 window covered by this unit. A student writing an AP long-essay response citing Cahokia as evidence for this unit's period should —
choices: skip discussing Cahokia altogether in this response, since Mississippian sites like it fall outside the AP World History curriculum's American units
treat Cahokia as a Mexica administrative outpost, since Mexica tribute networks reached north from central Mexico into the Mississippi River valley
place Cahokia's peak population squarely inside the 1200-1450 window, since Mississippian mound-building there continued at full scale through the fifteenth century
cite Cahokia as evidence of complex, hierarchical urban society in North America before European contact, dating its peak to before this unit's window
hints: Cahokia's peak (1050-1200) is a genuine chronological outlier relative to this unit's 1200-1450 window — precision about timing matters on the AP exam.
Rule out any answer erasing Cahokia's relevance altogether or wrongly linking it to Mexica administration — it was an independent Mississippian society.

problemText: By 1200, the Dar al-Islam — the collective territories under Muslim rule and cultural influence — stretched from Iberia and North Africa through the Middle East into Central and South Asia. Which statement best describes its political structure at that time?
choices: It was a religiously and culturally connected zone made up of many competing, independently ruled states
It was a single, unified political empire ruled directly by one caliph in Baghdad
It had no shared religious or intellectual institutions connecting its different regions
It remained confined to the Arabian Peninsula only, with no meaningful presence in Iberia, Africa, or Asia
hints: Even by 1200, real political power in the Dar al-Islam was already spread across many regional rulers, not concentrated in Baghdad.
Rule out any answer denying the ulama/madrasa/Sufi networks that did connect the region religiously and intellectually.

problemText: The Seljuk Sultanate (from the eleventh century), the Delhi Sultanate (established 1206), and the Mamluk Sultanate (from 1250) each exercised real, independent Muslim political power in different regions of the Dar al-Islam. The existence of these three states before and shortly after 1258 is best used as evidence that —
choices: each of these three states formally answered to Baghdad's caliph for all military and tax decisions
the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad had already lost most practical political power well before the Mongols sacked the city in 1258
Muslim political power did not exist anywhere outside Baghdad's caliphal court until the Mongols destroyed the city in 1258
these three states were established only after the Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, filling the resulting power vacuum
hints: Seljuk rule began in the eleventh century and the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 — both well before Baghdad fell in 1258.
Rule out any answer requiring these states to answer to Baghdad, or claiming Muslim political power began only after 1258.

problemText: In 1260, Mamluk forces defeated a Mongol army at the Battle of Ain Jalut, just two years after the Mongols had sacked Baghdad and executed the last Abbasid caliph residing there. This Mamluk victory is best used as evidence for which point about the Dar al-Islam after 1258?
choices: Muslim political power across the whole Dar al-Islam collapsed the moment the Baghdad caliphate finally fell in 1258
the Mongol army that sacked Baghdad went on to conquer Mamluk Egypt within the following decade
an independent Muslim state could check Mongol expansion and continue exercising real political-military power after Baghdad's fall
the Mamluks required the Abbasid caliph's approval before engaging Mongol forces in battle
hints: Ain Jalut happened only two years after Baghdad fell — think about what a Mamluk victory that soon shows about Muslim political power's survival.
Rule out any answer treating Baghdad's fall as ending Muslim political-military capacity everywhere.

problemText: Champa rice, a fast-ripening, drought-resistant variety introduced into Song China from what is now Vietnam, allowed farmers to bring in multiple harvests within a single year. Which outcome is most directly associated with this agricultural change?
choices: a sharp, sustained decline in China's total population
the collapse of Song China's civil-service examination system
the introduction of paper currency to replace grain as a medium of exchange
substantial population growth supporting an increasingly commercialized, urbanized economy
hints: More harvests per year directly increases the food supply available to support a growing population.
Rule out any answer linking rice farming to the exam system or to paper currency — those are separate Song-era developments.

problemText: Under feudalism in medieval Europe, monarchs granted land (fiefs) to nobles in exchange for military service and loyalty, and those nobles could in turn grant land to lesser lords. Which statement best describes the kind of political power this system produced?
choices: a decentralized structure in which political and military authority radiated outward through personal, reciprocal bonds rather than a trained central administration
a highly centralized bureaucracy in which officials were selected by a standardized examination
a system in which the Catholic Church held no independent political or economic power
an economic arrangement in which peasants owned their manor's land outright, free of any obligation to a lord
hints: Compare feudalism's personal, reciprocal bonds to the centralized bureaucracies studied elsewhere in this unit.
Rule out any answer describing an exam-selected bureaucracy or a powerless Church — neither matches feudal Europe.

problemText: Medieval Europe's revival of merchant towns and universities (Paris, Oxford, Bologna) from the eleventh-twelfth century onward built institutional centers of commerce and higher learning, even as political power in Europe remained fragmented among competing kings, feudal nobles, and the Church. Which conclusion about this revival is best supported by comparing it to the Islamic world's ulama/madrasa network covered elsewhere in this unit?
choices: Medieval Europe's fragmented political structure prevented any independent town or university from forming without direct royal or papal sponsorship
Europe's towns and universities show that political fragmentation did not prevent building its own institutions of commerce and scholarship
European universities adopted the madrasa's curriculum and legal-training model wholesale from the Dar al-Islam's scholarly network
the rise of universities shows that the Catholic Church had already lost its independent authority over higher education well before 1450
hints: The core point is that fragmented political power did not prevent Europe from building its own institutions — a different, not a lesser, track.
Rule out any answer claiming Europe built nothing, that Europe copied the madrasa system directly, or that the Church lost authority over education.

problemText: The Delhi Sultanate, established in 1206, was a series of Turkic and Afghan Muslim dynasties ruling much of North India. Which statement best describes the religious composition of the population it governed?
choices: a population that had overwhelmingly converted to Islam under Sultanate rule
a population composed mostly of Buddhist subjects under a rival Buddhist dynasty
a population that remained majority Hindu throughout Sultanate rule
a population with no religious diversity at all prior to the Sultanate's founding
hints: The Delhi Sultanate extended Muslim political rule by conquest, but that is a separate question from the population's actual religious composition.
Rule out any answer claiming mass conversion or religious uniformity — neither matches the historical record.

problemText: Angkor Wat, the Khmer Empire's monumental temple complex, was built in the early twelfth century originally as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, and was later adapted for Buddhist worship. A student using Angkor Wat as evidence in an AP World History response should describe it as illustrating —
choices: a temple built only for Buddhist worship, with no Hindu iconography anywhere in its original twelfth-century design
the Delhi Sultanate's Turkic Muslim rulers extended direct political and religious control over mainland Southeast Asian courts
a long-standing absence of Hindu religious influence anywhere across mainland Southeast Asia during the medieval period
the religious layering typical of Southeast Asia, where one monumental site shifted between Hindu and Buddhist use over time
hints: Angkor Wat's own history — Hindu origin, later Buddhist adaptation — is itself the evidence of religious layering, not a single fixed tradition.
Rule out any answer erasing its Hindu origins or wrongly connecting it to the Delhi Sultanate's political reach.
